title: Platform Engineering in the Age of AI
gist: In an InfoQ Live roundtable, platform engineering leaders from DKB, Shine/sevDesk, and Harness argue AI is not replacing platform engineering fundamentals but is shifting the bottleneck from writing code to the deployment/governance loop, forcing more standardization (not less) because non-deterministic agent output demands stronger guardrails, and pushing platform teams to become context-and-governance layers (MCP servers, internal skills, agent permissions) rather than infrastructure gatekeepers.

themes.theme: Where AI is already delivering value for platform teams

insights.claim: Davide de Paolis says AI's biggest early win is clearing chronically neglected but important work — documentation, boilerplate, diagrams, and recurring Infrastructure-as-Code changes across multiple repos — that was previously deprioritized under roadmap and OKR pressure because it was never urgent.
insights.speaker: Davide de Paolis
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-risk near-term AI ROI category (neglected maintenance work) that platform teams can point to for quick wins before tackling harder autonomous-agent governance questions.
insights.quote: Everything that was neglected is now accomplished.
insights.locator: section 'Intersection of AI and Platform Engineering', Davide de Paolis's first answer

insights.claim: Davide de Paolis's platform team manages roughly 100 AWS accounts and hundreds of repositories with Terraform, and uses AI to run discovery across that landscape — finding differences, establishing baselines, and aggregating data to decide what to work on next.
insights.speaker: Davide de Paolis
insights.so_what: A concrete scale benchmark (100 AWS accounts, hundreds of repos) for what AI-assisted infrastructure discovery looks like in a mid-size platform org — useful comparator for sizing similar tooling investments elsewhere.
insights.quote: My team manages around 100 AWS accounts and overlooks hundreds of repositories with Terraform.
insights.locator: section 'Intersection of AI and Platform Engineering', Davide de Paolis's first answer

insights.claim: Providing internal MCP servers or agent skills lets platform teams offload first-line developer support: an AI configured against the team's own MCP server can answer routine questions or generate code directly, reducing the support burden that would otherwise fall on the platform team.
insights.speaker: Davide de Paolis
insights.so_what: Internal MCP servers are emerging as the concrete product platform teams build to scale themselves — a pattern worth tracking as a category (internal agent tooling / dev-platform MCP infrastructure) for infra vendors and buyers alike.
insights.quote: The AI configured to use our own MCP server or our own agent can answer the first line of questions or produce immediately some code that otherwise we would need to do ourselves.
insights.locator: section 'Intersection of AI and Platform Engineering', Davide de Paolis's first answer

themes.theme: What AI does not change, and where the bottleneck actually moved

insights.claim: Stephane Di Cesare argues platform engineering's core principles are unchanged by AI — it is 'just a new way to do automation' — but the scale changes because platforms must now serve workloads originating from agents as well as humans, making clear service intent and clear APIs more important than before.
insights.speaker: Stephane Di Cesare
insights.so_what: Pushes back on hype narratives that AI reinvents platform engineering — useful corrective for evaluating vendor claims that a product 'reinvents' DevOps/platform practice rather than scaling it.
insights.quote: I think what's important to realize is that platform engineering is still there. AI is just an extra tool that came up.
insights.locator: section 'Intersection of AI and Platform Engineering', Stephane Di Cesare's answer

insights.claim: As AI shrinks the time needed to generate code, the bottleneck shifts to the outer loop — deployment, security scans, and governance gates — creating pressure on platform teams to enable machine-speed self-service because leadership questions why heavy AI tooling investment isn't reaching production faster.
insights.speaker: Stephen Cihak
insights.so_what: Identifies where investment should shift for platform/DevOps tooling vendors: value is migrating from code-generation tools (increasingly commoditized) to deployment-gate, security-scan, and governance automation — the new bottleneck to sell into.
insights.quote: It needs to operate at machine speed versus human speed. A lot of platform paved paths have manual phase gates and things like that that really slow down the process.
insights.locator: section 'Intersection of AI and Platform Engineering', Stephen Cihak's answer

insights.claim: Camila Macedo observes that AI is accelerating the discovery of security vulnerabilities faster than open-source maintainers can patch them, making maintainers feel perpetually behind even as AI also helps process previously unstructured data like logs for debugging.
insights.speaker: Camila Macedo
insights.so_what: A vulnerability-discovery/patch-velocity mismatch driven by AI is a second-order security risk for the open-source supply chain broadly — relevant to any company dependent on OSS maintenance capacity, since AI is accelerating one side of the race (finding) without necessarily accelerating the other (fixing).
insights.quote: Nowadays, AI is helping people find so many security issues.
insights.locator: section 'Intersection of AI and Platform Engineering', Camila Macedo's answer

themes.theme: Guardrails, governance, and who is accountable for agent decisions

insights.claim: Camila Macedo cites Anthropic's Opus 5 benchmark showing 25% to 65% accuracy with regard to code as evidence that current AI models cannot yet be trusted to make autonomous decisions in high-stakes domains like banking, and expresses relief that her bank (DKB) keeps humans, not agents, making decisions on security, legal, and compliance matters.
insights.speaker: Camila Macedo
insights.so_what: A specific, named accuracy range (25-65%) for a frontier coding model cited by a practicing engineer as grounds for withholding autonomous decision authority from AI in regulated environments — directly relevant to any investment thesis assuming near-term autonomous-agent adoption in banking/finance.
insights.quote: Anthropic from Opus 5, the benchmark is like 25% to 65% of accuracy with regards to code. We cannot really trust in the decisions that are taken by AI.
insights.locator: section 'Example Developer Platforms (Internal/Open-Source)', Camila Macedo's closing remark

insights.claim: Davide de Paolis frames AI governance for platform teams as encompassing reusable context management (code conventions, PR-creation skills, ticketing integrations with Jira or Linear), safety guardrails against agents 'going rogue' or hallucinating with too much initiative, and FinOps controls over tool licensing, token overage costs, and which MCP servers agents are permitted to use.
insights.speaker: Davide de Paolis
insights.so_what: A concrete three-part governance scope (context distribution, behavioral guardrails, FinOps/tool licensing) that defines the emerging 'AI governance' product category platform teams are building or buying into — a checklist for evaluating AI-governance tooling vendors.
insights.quote: What MCP server can be used by the agents? Do we want to block them or allow only some of them?
insights.locator: section 'Adapting the Internal Developer Platform to the AI Era', Davide de Paolis's second answer

insights.claim: Camila Macedo argues AI/agent security should follow the exact same principles historically applied to human access: least privilege, clear permissions, strong policy, and strong auditing — treating agents as just another category of actor needing the same controls, not a fundamentally new problem.
insights.speaker: Camila Macedo
insights.so_what: A reusable investment-diligence lens: a vendor's 'AI security' framework that reinvents access-control concepts rather than extending least-privilege/auditing to agents may be over-engineering or marketing novelty rather than solving the real problem.
insights.quote: Things like least privilege, clear permissions, a strong policy, and to have a very good auditing is still more essential than ever.
insights.locator: section 'Adapting the Internal Developer Platform to the AI Era', Camila Macedo's answer

insights.claim: Stephen Cihak warns that third-party model providers can silently change the underlying model, producing unexpected drift in agent outputs; teams that don't continuously monitor responses and run post-production AI evaluations will be caught off guard when a previously reliable behavior changes without notice.
insights.speaker: Stephen Cihak
insights.so_what: A concrete operational risk (silent model swaps by vendors) that argues for building continuous model-output evaluation/monitoring into any production agent pipeline — a product gap for AI-observability vendors and a due-diligence question for any company relying on third-party model APIs.
insights.quote: I've seen it where the model is changed underneath you silently. If you're not monitoring those responses on a regular basis, you can get various results that you were not expecting
insights.locator: section 'Standards, Governance, and Guardrails with AI', Stephen Cihak's answer

insights.claim: Stephen Cihak argues AI's non-deterministic nature (the same prompt can produce 14 different implementations) is itself the reason AI is driving more, not less, demand for platform standards and guardrails, since governance is how you make non-deterministic tooling predictable.
insights.speaker: Stephen Cihak
insights.so_what: Counters a naive assumption that AI reduces the need for platform standardization — instead it's argued to increase it, which supports continued/increased investment in platform-governance tooling even as coding itself gets automated.
insights.quote: you can put the one prompt in and it's going to come up with 14 different ways to do it.
insights.locator: section 'Standards, Governance, and Guardrails with AI', Stephen Cihak's answer

themes.theme: The autonomous SDLC vision and its governance requirements

insights.claim: Stephen Cihak predicts a near-future autonomous SDLC where agents detect a bug, diagnose the code, build and submit the fix as a PR, and other agents deploy and verify it — with governance systems producing auditable evidence of every decision, replacing slower human review structures like a weekly Change Advisory Board that cannot keep pace with agent-driven change velocity.
insights.speaker: Stephen Cihak
insights.so_what: A specific, concrete prediction (agent-to-agent bug-fix-to-deploy pipelines replacing weekly CAB reviews) that investors in DevOps/governance tooling should track as a leading indicator — vendors building auditable agent-decision evidence trails are positioned for this shift.
insights.quote: you have other agents that go through the process of then deploying and ensuring there's no vulnerabilities and that it's working right.
insights.locator: section 'The AI and Human Aspects of Developer Platforms', Stephen Cihak's first answer

insights.claim: Stephane Di Cesare insists that despite increasing agent autonomy, a human always remains behind the decision of what intent the platform and its agents should pursue — the scale of execution changes, but deciding the goal stays a human responsibility, not the agent's.
insights.speaker: Stephane Di Cesare
insights.so_what: Establishes a normative boundary (humans set intent, agents execute) that is likely to become a compliance/governance design requirement in regulated industries — a useful test for evaluating whether a vendor's 'autonomous agent' product actually preserves human decision authority or quietly removes it.
insights.quote: What you want to reach is still your decision and not the agent's decision. Also, for even how autonomous agents are, this is part of your decision.
insights.locator: section 'The AI and Human Aspects of Developer Platforms', Stephane Di Cesare's second answer

insights.claim: Davide de Paolis notes an ironic second-order effect: teams have always known they needed proper documentation and specifications for humans, but only now that agents hallucinate or miss context are organizations actually investing in documentation and knowledge graphs — a byproduct that benefits both agents and human engineers simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Davide de Paolis
insights.so_what: Identifies a real, positive-externality use case for AI adoption budgets: agent-context requirements are forcing overdue documentation investment that improves human-team velocity too — a soft ROI argument for AI infrastructure spend beyond direct productivity.
insights.quote: Only now that we have agents, only now that we have agents hallucinating or missing the context, we are focusing on improving the documentation, making the knowledge graph, so that the agents can work properly.
insights.locator: section 'The AI and Human Aspects of Developer Platforms', Davide de Paolis's second answer

insights.claim: Davide de Paolis reports that when a developer uses agent orchestration to run spec-driven development across multiple tickets simultaneously, the resulting surge of PRs bottlenecks on his platform team's GitHub runner capacity, since the platform is responsible for sustaining the CI pipeline load at this new agent-driven scale.
insights.speaker: Davide de Paolis
insights.so_what: A concrete new capacity-planning constraint (CI runner throughput) introduced by multi-ticket agent orchestration — infra teams should proactively size CI compute for agent-driven PR volume rather than assuming historical human-pace baselines hold.
insights.quote: Now, if a developer is very advanced and uses agent orchestration, so he's able to run spec-driven development on multiple tickets at once, we have this bottleneck of a lot of PRs.
insights.locator: section 'The AI and Human Aspects of Developer Platforms', Davide de Paolis's third answer

themes.theme: Equal footing and the changing role of developers vs platform engineers

insights.claim: Stephane Di Cesare observes that historically platform engineers were better at Terraform than most developers, giving platform teams a natural authority; with AI, developers and platform engineers now start from the same footing on infrastructure code, requiring platform teams to shift toward a contribution model where they collaborate with developers rather than dictate solutions.
insights.speaker: Stephane Di Cesare
insights.so_what: A structural shift in platform-team authority and value proposition: expertise-based gatekeeping erodes as AI levels infrastructure-coding skill, so platform teams must justify their role via governance/context curation rather than raw technical superiority — relevant to how platform-engineering roles and headcount evolve.
insights.quote: Now, with AI, the thing is we're all on an equal footing. We have to help the developers with AI, but developers and platform teams are all starting with AI.
insights.locator: section 'Adapting the Internal Developer Platform to the AI Era', Stephane Di Cesare's second answer

insights.claim: Stephane Di Cesare notes AI has generally lowered the bar for technical work, letting people previously outside technical roles build things themselves; the value platform engineers add is their operations background, i.e., recognizing that the real challenge is not building something but being accountable for maintaining it — illustrated by his own AI-assisted frontend work producing 'crazy' code like inline HTML in components that even an incompetent frontend developer could see was unmaintainable.
insights.speaker: Stephane Di Cesare
insights.so_what: A specific, credible first-person example of AI-generated code that 'works' but is maintenance-unsound — supports the broader investment thesis that AI expands who can produce code but does not remove the need for specialist review/maintainability judgment.
insights.quote: The AI was doing some very crazy things that even for a quite incompetent developer in frontend as I am, I could see that probably including HTML directly in frontend components is not a good idea.
insights.locator: section 'The Changing Role of Devs and Platform Engineers in the Age of AI', Stephane Di Cesare's answer

insights.claim: Camila Macedo argues, using the historical analogy of compilers not eliminating engineering jobs, that AI will not eliminate engineering roles either but is instead another layer of abstraction; she predicts continued demand for people who can understand, maintain, and troubleshoot systems even as AI becomes very good at generating code, alongside new job categories emerging around the technology itself.
insights.speaker: Camila Macedo
insights.so_what: A direct counter to job-displacement narratives from a practicing engineer, using a historical technology-adoption analogy (compilers) — relevant context for labor-market and hiring-demand assumptions embedded in AI-driven software-productivity investment theses.
insights.quote: In the same way that the compilers didn't take the engineering developer jobs, I don't think AI will do the same.
insights.locator: section 'AI and The Future of Platform Eng', Camila Macedo's answer

insights.claim: Stephen Cihak reframes the future of platform engineering as task displacement rather than job displacement, arguing platform engineering becomes more critical, not less, as organizations push toward a fully autonomous SDLC that requires heavy governance and evidence generation, especially for regulatory compliance.
insights.speaker: Stephen Cihak
insights.so_what: Suggests platform-engineering headcount and tooling investment should grow, not shrink, as agent autonomy increases — a counter-signal to assumptions that AI reduces total platform-engineering spend.
insights.quote: I don't necessarily see job displacement as opposed to task displacement in platform engineering. I think platform engineering becomes more and more critical as the world continues to move into the space.
insights.locator: section 'AI and The Future of Platform Eng', Stephen Cihak's closing answer

insights.claim: Stephen Cihak uses a highway-versus-freeway analogy to argue that supporting machine-speed agent-driven development requires investing in fundamentally stronger, larger governance structures (like freeways separating traffic to allow higher speeds safely) rather than incrementally patching existing human-paced processes (like two-lane highways).
insights.speaker: Stephen Cihak
insights.so_what: A memorable mental model for why AI-era platform investment needs structural redesign rather than incremental tooling — useful for framing capex/opex conversations about platform re-architecture versus point-solution AI tooling purchases.
insights.quote: Then they built these freeways where traffic is separated and you can go significantly faster. You have to build stronger, larger structures to allow things to go faster.
insights.locator: section 'AI and The Future of Platform Eng', Stephen Cihak's closing answer

themes.theme: Measuring platform success in the AI era

insights.claim: Stephane Di Cesare admits there is no solved answer for measuring whether platform engineering reduces cognitive load — it remains subjective, and DKB's current focus is increasing developer trust enough that they give honest feedback, since developers have historically viewed the platform team as 'the ops team who says no.'
insights.speaker: Stephane Di Cesare
insights.so_what: Highlights that platform-engineering ROI/success metrics remain immature industry-wide even at a large bank — a caution against overconfident 'platform engineering productivity' metrics cited in vendor pitches or case studies.
insights.quote: we've seen that developers have had the tendency to see the platform team as the ops team and also as the team who says, no.
insights.locator: section 'Measuring the Success of an Internal Platform', Stephane Di Cesare's answer

insights.claim: Davide de Paolis uses onboarding time as his primary concrete success metric: reducing the time for a team to go from idea to production (setup, configuration, deployment, pipeline selection) from three weeks to one hour via a reusable platform solution directly demonstrates reduced cognitive load, supplemented by tracking Slack/PR back-and-forth volume as a proxy for documentation gaps, and DORA metrics before/after platform team creation.
insights.speaker: Davide de Paolis
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified example (3 weeks to 1 hour onboarding) and a specific metrics stack (onboarding time, communication back-and-forth volume, DORA before/after) that gives investors and platform-tooling buyers a template for evaluating internal-platform ROI claims elsewhere.
insights.quote: If there are multiple teams that need to take three weeks to deploy something on a Kubernetes cluster or on Fargate, and we can remove that work and provide a reusable solution, a ready-made solution that brings that down to one hour
insights.locator: section 'Measuring the Success of an Internal Platform', Davide de Paolis's answer
